The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A and carbon dioxide - true statement is:

options.label: A
options.text: Involves the participation of lipoic acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Is activated when pyruvate decarboxylase of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC) is phosphorylated by PDH kinase in the presence of ATP.

questions.answerText: Involves the participation of lipoic acid.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans.  A) Involves the participation of lipoic acid.

 

The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and CO₂ is catalyzed by the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDC or PDHC) in the mitochondrial matrix. This is a crucial irreversible link between glycolysis and the TCA cycle.

 

A. Involves the participation of lipoic acid – Correct

 

  • The PDH complex has three core enzymes:
    1. E1: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (decarboxylation)
    2. E2: Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase
    3. E3: Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase
  • Lipoic acid is a coenzyme for PDH complex

 

Other Option:

 

Option B. Is activated when pyruvate decarboxylase of the PDHC is phosphorylated by PDH kinase in the presence of ATP

 

  • This is incorrect.
  • Phosphorylation by PDH kinase INACTIVATES the PDH complex.

 

Option C. Is reversible

 

  • The PDH reaction is irreversible under physiological conditions.
  • Acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate in mammals.
  • That’s why fatty acids (via acetyl-CoA) cannot be used to make glucose.

 

Option D. Occurs in the cytosol

 

  • The PDH complex resides in the mitochondrial matrix, not the cytosol.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by the PDH complex is irreversible, occurs in the mitochondria, and involves several cofactors:

 

  • TPP (vitamin B1)
  • Lipoic acid
  • FAD
  • NAD⁺
  • Coenzyme A

questions.stem: Under conditions of anaerobic glycolysis, the NAD+ required by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase is supplied by a reaction catalyzed by which of the following enzymes?
Which of the following enzymes is common for both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glucose-6-phosphatase

 

Glucose-6-phosphatase:

 

  • Catalyzes: Glucose-6-phosphate → Glucose
  • Present in liver and kidney, not in muscle
  • Common to both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis

 

Glucose-6-phosphatase is the final enzyme in both:

 

  • Glycogenolysis – the breakdown of glycogen to glucose
  • Gluconeogenesis – the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors

 

It removes the phosphate group from glucose-6-phosphate, producing free glucose that can be released into the bloodstream — primarily in the liver and kidney, but not in muscle (muscle lacks this enzyme).

 

Other Option:

 

Option A. Hexokinase

 

  • Catalyzes: Glucose → Glucose-6-phosphate
  • Used in glycolysis, not in glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis

 

Option C. Phosphoglucomutase

 

  • Catalyzes: Glucose-1-phosphate ↔ Glucose-6-phosphate
  • Used in glycogenolysis and glycogenesis, not in gluconeogenesis

 

Option D. Glucokinase

 

  • Liver-specific enzyme for glucose → glucose-6-phosphate
  • Part of glycolysis, not involved in gluconeogenesis or glycogenolysis

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glucose-6-phosphatase is a key enzyme for releasing free glucose into the bloodstream and is shared by both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, making it essential for maintaining blood glucose during fasting.

 

Phosphoglucomutase is common in glycogenolysis and glycogenesis

A 9-month-old infant, is brought to the pediatric clinic by her concerned parents with history of generalized fits. Baby had delayed milestone and was lethargic, hair was grey colored and skin was light colored. Mother gave the history of mousy odor in the urine. On IQ assessment patient has intellectual disability. In one of the following rare variants of PKU The enzyme deficient is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dihydropterin Reductase

 

The patient's symptoms – generalized fits, delayed milestones, lethargy, grey-colored hair, light-colored skin, a characteristic "mousy odor" in the urine, and intellectual disability – are all highly indicative of Phenylketonuria (PKU).

 

PKU is primarily caused by a deficiency in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. However, the question specifically asks about a "rare variant of PKU."

 

Hyperphenylalaninemia, the biochemical hallmark of PKU, can also be caused by "rare deficiencies in any of the several enzymes required to synthesize BH4 or in dihydropteridine reductase". Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is a crucial coenzyme for PAH. If dihydropteridine reductase, the enzyme responsible for regenerating BH4 from its oxidized form (BH2), is deficient, then PAH cannot function effectively, leading to the accumulation of phenylalanine and a clinical picture similar to classic PKU. 

 

Therefore, a deficiency in Dihydro pterin Reductase fits the description of an enzyme involved in a "rare variant of PKU."

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Histidine decarboxylase: This enzyme is involved in the conversion of histidine to histamine. It has no direct association with phenylalanine metabolism or PKU symptoms as described in the sources.

 

Option B. Phenylalanine Hydroxylase (PAH): While a deficiency in PAH causes classic PKU, the question specifically asks about a "rare variant." Deficiencies in enzymes that affect BH4 metabolism (like dihydropteridine reductase) are considered "rare variants" that indirectly cause the same biochemical problem as a direct PAH deficiency.

 

Option D. Tyrosine Kinase: Tyrosine kinase is an enzyme involved in signal transduction pathways, phosphorylating tyrosine residues on proteins. The sources mention tyrosine in the context of melanin production via tyrosinase (which is decreased in PKU leading to hypopigmentation), but not tyrosine kinase as an enzyme deficient in PKU or its variants.

questions.stem: In Hyper Ammonia Type I there is increase ammonia due to deficiency of CPS-I, ammonia is toxic to brain by decreasing the following substrate of TCA cycle:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) α-Ketoglutarate 

 

In Hyperammonemia Type I, there is a deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I), the first enzyme in the urea cycle, which is located in the mitochondria.

 

  • CPS-I catalyzes:
    Ammonia + CO₂ + ATP → Carbamoyl phosphate
  • When CPS-I is deficient → ammonia accumulates in the blood.

 

Ammonia exerts its neurotoxicity primarily by depleting α-ketoglutarate:

 

  • Ammonia + α-ketoglutarate → Glutamate
  • Further ammonia converts glutamate → Glutamine

 

This process leads to:

 

  1. Depletion of α-ketoglutarate, a key intermediate of the TCA cycle
  2. Impaired energy metabolism in neurons
  3. Cerebral edema and neurologic symptoms

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Succinyl CoA:

 

  • Not directly affected by ammonia toxicity
  • A downstream TCA intermediate

 

Option C. Oxaloacetate:

 

  • May be secondarily affected if the TCA cycle slows, but not the primary target of ammonia toxicity

 

Option D. Fumarate:

 

  • Also a downstream TCA intermediate
  • Not directly involved in ammonia detoxification

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hyperammonemia leads to neurotoxicity by depleting α-ketoglutarate, thereby inhibiting the TCA cycle in brain cells and impairing ATP production.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about DNA polymerase except:

options.label: B
options.text: Beta polymerase has no proof reading

options.label: C
options.text: DNA G protein has primase activity in E. Coli

options.label: D
options.text: DNA polymerase two has no proof reading

questions.answerText: DNA polymerase two has no proof reading
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) DNA polymerase two has no proof reading

 

DNA polymerases are essential enzymes for DNA replication and repair, both in eukaryotes and prokaryotes. The question includes details from both systems (eukaryotic and E. coli).

 

Option D: DNA polymerase two has no proofreading

 

  • DNA polymerase II (E. coli) has:
    • 3’→5’ exonuclease activity → allows proofreading

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Alpha polymerase has primase activity

 

True (Eukaryotes)

 

  • DNA polymerase α is found in eukaryotes
  • It synthesize a short RNA primer

 

Option B: Beta polymerase has no proofreading

 

  • DNA polymerase β is involved in DNA repair
  • It lacks 3’→5’ exonuclease (proofreading) activity

 

Option C: DNA G protein has primase activity in E. coli

 

True (Prokaryotes)

 

  • DnaG is the primase enzyme in E. coli
  • Synthesizes short RNA primers needed for DNA polymerase III to begin elongation
